quirks: Civil (Statutory) registration in Scotland began at the registration-district level on 1 January 1855, not before; for marriages before that date the only official record is the Old Parochial Register (OPR) of the Church of Scotland or a nonconformist congregation's own register.

Campbeltown OPR marriage registers 1820-1854 are on microfilm 1041005 (FS Library), and the name index covering marriages 1681-1854 is on microfiche 6900069 at the FamilySearch Library. The full index is also searchable by name on ScotlandsPeople.gov.uk for a small fee.

Campbeltown parish had two separate congregations — Lowland (English-speaking) and Highland (Gaelic-speaking) — each recording baptisms and marriages in the same OPR volumes but in separate sequences. A couple belonging to either congregation would appear in the relevant sequence, not necessarily the one searched first.

By the 19th century a majority of Campbeltown's population was nonconformist. The Relief Church (later United Presbyterian, ref CH3/1421) and the Free Church (Lochend, ref CH3/1047) were both active throughout 1820-1860; a marriage or baptism in one of these congregations will NOT appear in the OPR at all.
Roman Catholic records for Campbeltown do not survive before 1879 — no early Catholic vital records are known extant.

Kirk session minutes (CH2/50, minutes 1821-1890) are digitized and full-text searchable on FamilySearch; they record discipline cases, poor relief, and sometimes mention marriages and irregular unions that do not appear in the OPR itself.

The 1855 Statutory marriage certificate is uniquely detailed — it recorded birthplaces of bride and groom and names and ages of both parents. Even if a couple married in 1855 rather than before, this certificate alone can supply two generations of ancestry.

Scottish naming customs followed a strong generational pattern: first son typically named after paternal grandfather, second son after maternal grandfather. Neil (1850) and James (1852) may therefore point to the surnames of the two grandfathers.

Probate jurisdiction: Campbeltown was under the Commissary Court of Argyll until 1823, then the Sheriff's Court of Dunoon. Records 1513-1901 are indexed on ScotlandsPeople; pre-1823 originals are on FamilySearch microfilm.

The Neglected Entries Register (late-registered events approximately 1820-1860, registered 1860-1868) is on microfilm and digitized in the FamilySearch Catalog — worth checking if a marriage or birth cannot be found in the standard OPR or Statutory series.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Campbeltown, Argyllshire, Scotland (1820–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Parish number:** 507 (Quoad Omnia Parish)
- **Historic county:** Argyllshire
- **Ecclesiastical jurisdiction:** Presbytery of Kintyre, Synod of Argyll
- **Civil registration district:** Campbeltown (from 1 January 1855)
- **Sheriff Court:** Campbeltown (also Dunoon, Fort William, Inveraray, Oban, Tobermory)
- **Commissary Court:** Argyll (until 1823), then Sheriff's Court of Dunoon
- **Population during period:** 8,706 (1795); 9,539 (1841) — source: New Statistical Account of Scotland (1843), cited at [Campbeltown, Argyllshire, Scotland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Campbeltown,_Argyllshire,_Scotland_Genealogy)
- **Economy:** Fishing, farming, distilling (Campbeltown was a major whisky centre), some maritime trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Scottish; the town had two distinct congregations reflecting a Lowland (English-speaking) and Highland (Gaelic-speaking) population
- **Religious denominations:** Church of Scotland (two charges — English and Gaelic); Relief Church (later United Presbyterian); United Secession Church (1831–1847); Free Church (from 1843); Independent Church (1805–c.1864); Roman Catholic (church formed 1816); St Kieran's Episcopal Church
- **Key historical events:** Disruption of 1843 (split of the Church of Scotland, creating the Free Church); expansion of herring fishing industry; growth of Campbeltown distilling

## Boundary changes
- The parish of Campbeltown (#507) was formed from the ancient parishes of Kilkerran, Kilmichael, and Kilchousland, united after the Reformation under the name Lochhead, then renamed Campbelton around 1687.
- Boundaries were stable throughout the 1820–1860 period. The parish also served as the civil registration district when Statutory registration began on 1 January 1855.
- No county-level boundary change affected this parish during the target period.

## Available record types

### Vital records — civil (Statutory) registration
- **Start date:** 1 January 1855, at the registration-district level, per [Scotland Civil Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Scotland_Civil_Registration)
- **What exists:** Birth, marriage, and death registers for Campbeltown district 507, from 1855. Digitized volumes found: births 1855–1860 (6 separate annual volumes), marriages 1855–1859 (5 volumes), deaths 1855–1860 (6 volumes).
- **Digitization status:** These volumes show 0 images and 0% name-indexed in FamilySearch's volume search — they are held in the FamilySearch catalog but accessible only at a FamilySearch Center or Affiliate Library, or via ScotlandsPeople. ScotlandsPeople has indexed and imaged Campbeltown marriages 1855–1947, births 1855–1922, deaths 1855–1972.
- **Where held online:** ScotlandsPeople.gov.uk (subscription, approximately £7.50 for 30 credits; each image costs 6 credits). FamilySearch has indexed extracts for 1855–1875, 1881, and 1891 in the [Scotland, Civil Registration collection (5000163)](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/5000163); images of those years can be browsed at a FamilySearch Center.
- **The 1855 marriage certificate is uniquely rich:** it recorded birthplaces of bride and groom, and names and ages of both parents — enough to extend a pedigree two full generations from a single document.
- **Gaps:** Civil registration did not exist before 1 January 1855. Marriages before that date are not in this series.

### Vital records — Old Parochial Registers (OPR) (pre-1855)
- **Record level:** Parish (Church of Scotland, Campbeltown parish #507)
- **Births/baptisms:** 1659–1855 across three main film groups:
  - Film 1041003: 1659–1773 (Lowland) and Gaelic congregation from June 1728
  - Film 1041004: 1682–1822
  - Film 1041005: 1776–1855 (volume 6, covering 1820–1839 baptisms, 1820–1854 marriages, 1817–1854 burials)
- **Marriages:** 1681–1854 (same film groups). The key volume for 1820–1854 marriages is film **1041005**, which covers OPR volume 6. This is the primary source for any marriage of Hugh Mclachlan and Catharine Muir if they wed before 1855.
- **Deaths/burials:** Very sparse — only about 20 entries before 1808, and only 32 entries for 1817–1854. Do not rely on burial records to confirm or rule out events.
- **Digitization:** The OPR volumes on microfilm are **browse-only** at a FamilySearch Center (0% name-indexed in the FamilySearch volume system). However, the **name index** to Campbeltown marriages 1681–1854 has been extracted and is:
  - Searchable free of charge in [Scotland Marriages, 1561–1910](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1771074) on FamilySearch
  - Searchable on ScotlandsPeople.gov.uk (fee to view the image)
  - Available on microfiche 6900069 at the FamilySearch Library ("Marriages, A thru Z, 1681–1854, 3 microfiches")
- **Important warning:** Registration in Church of Scotland registers was costly and unpopular. By the 19th century an estimated 30% of events in some urban parishes were not recorded. A couple not found in the OPR index may simply not have registered — not may not have married.
- **Two congregations:** The Lowland (English) and Highland (Gaelic) series are recorded separately within the same volumes. Both series are included in the OPR index, but if searching by browsing the film, you must look in both sections.
- **Source page:** [Campbeltown, Argyllshire, Scotland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Campbeltown,_Argyllshire,_Scotland_Genealogy)

### Church records — nonconformist (pre- and post-1855)
By the 1840s a majority of Campbeltown's population was in nonconformist congregations. A marriage in one of these churches will NOT appear in the Church of Scotland OPR.

**Campbeltown Relief Church (later United Presbyterian, ref CH3/1421):**
- History: formed 1766 when members left the Established Church
- Records: various minutes 1767–1847; Communion Rolls 1838–1867; Young Communicants Rolls 1843–1877
- Digitized: multiple volumes (CH3/1421/1–16) are online at FamilySearch, fulltext searchable but not name-indexed (0% recordSearchablePercent). These include session minutes 1755–1836, 1812–1835, 1836–1837, 1837–1841, 1842–1847; school records 1852–1874; communicants rolls 1829–1877.
- Held: National Archives of Scotland (NAS), Edinburgh

**Lochend Free Church (ref CH3/1047):**
- History: formed in the Disruption of 1843 from the English and Gaelic collegiate charges; records begin 1841 (pre-Disruption non-intrusion committee)
- Records: Committee Minutes 1843–1868; Communion Roll 1843–1862; cash books; membership records
- Digitized: multiple volumes (CH3/1047/1, 4, 9, 11–13, 15–16) are online at FamilySearch, fulltext searchable but not name-indexed
- Held: NAS Edinburgh

**St Kieran's Episcopal Church:**
- Records: Baptisms 1848–1855, Marriages 1849–1853
- Held: Argyll and Bute Archives (listed in the Argyll and Bute Archives Family History Sources wiki page)

**Campbeltown United Secession Church (1831–1847):**
- Merged into United Presbyterian in 1847; extent of pre-1855 records unknown

**Campbeltown Independent Church (1805–c.1864):**
- Extent of records unknown; contact United Reformed Church, Scottish Synod Office, Glasgow

**Roman Catholic Church:**
- A church was formed 1816 and dedicated 1850. No records are known to survive before 1879.

**Note from [Scotland Church Records wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Scotland_Church_Records):** In 1855 the government called for all non-parochial registers to be deposited with the official archive. These are now managed by ScotlandsPeople. Before 1834, nonconformist ministers were not authorized to perform marriages without banns having been read first in the parish church.

### Kirk session records (Church of Scotland)
- Minutes 1821–1890 and Account book 1744–1810 (NAS ref CH2/50)
- Kirk sessions dealt with moral discipline, poor relief, education, and parish business. They record individuals who may not appear in any OPR event — including couples who appeared before the session for irregular marriage or prenuptial fornication.
- Digitized volumes:
  - CH2/50/1: Jan 1821–Sept 1836 (111 images, fulltext searchable)
  - CH2/50/2: Dec 1836–Sept 1842 (104 images, fulltext searchable)
  - CH2/50/3: Oct 1842–Apr 1868 (227 images, fulltext searchable)
  - CH2/50/10: Communion Roll Jul 1854–May 1901 (64 images, fulltext searchable)
- Available online at FamilySearch (browse/fulltext, not name-indexed); also at NAS Edinburgh

### Census records
- National census taken every 10 years. Individual enumeration began with 1841.
- **1841 Census:** Campbeltown (parish 507), film 1042715. FamilySearch volume search: 63% name-indexed (imageGroupNumber 004536125_003). Also indexed at ScotlandsPeople, Ancestry, FindMyPast, MyHeritage.
- **1851 Census:** Film 1042349. FamilySearch volume search: 78% name-indexed (imageGroupNumber 004033892_003). Also at ScotlandsPeople, Ancestry, FindMyPast, MyHeritage.
- **1861–1891:** On microfilm (films 103795, 103951, 203555, 208803); also on ScotlandsPeople and other platforms.
- **1901–1921:** ScotlandsPeople only (index and images, fee).
- Census records from 1851 onward list every household member with name, age, birthplace, relationship, and occupation — primary sources for establishing who was in the household in each decade.
- **Source:** [Campbeltown census catalog entry](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/629967)

### Probate and court records
- Campbeltown was under the **Commissary Court of Argyll** until 1823, then transferred to the **Sheriff's Court of Dunoon**.
- Probate records (wills and testaments) 1513–1901 are indexed free on ScotlandsPeople; copies cost a small fee.
- Pre-1823 records are on microfilm at the FamilySearch Library. Search the FamilySearch Catalog under Argyll / Probate Records for microfilm numbers.
- Post-1823 Argyll records: some are in the FamilySearch Library catalog; search under Argyll / Probate Records.
- For the research question, estate papers filed after a party died would confirm identity, name spouse, and may give marriage date.
- **Source:** [Campbeltown, Argyllshire, Scotland Genealogy — Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Campbeltown,_Argyllshire,_Scotland_Genealogy#Probate_Records)

### Poor law records
- Two digitized volumes at FamilySearch:
  - HR/67/1: May 1778–June 1821 (130 images, fulltext searchable)
  - HR/67/2: August 1852–August 1899 (81 images, fulltext searchable)
- The General Register of Poor names paupers receiving relief; an index to Campbeltown poor c.1860–1899 was compiled by Tommy and Margaret Semple and is held at Argyll and Bute Archives.
- A poorhouse served the parish; poorhouse records name individuals.

### Land records
- Scotland used a feudal land system with property conveyed by sasine (formal possession). The General Register of Sasines is the primary record of land transfers.
- Valuation Rolls (property owners and occupiers) began in Scotland from 1855; available on ScotlandsPeople.
- Land Tax rolls 1645–1831 are available online at [ScotlandsPlaces](https://scotlandsplaces.gov.uk/digital-volumes/historical-tax-rolls/land-tax-rolls-1645-1831).
- Scottish Post Office Directories (1773–1911) are digitized at the National Library of Scotland ([digital.nls.uk/directories/](https://digital.nls.uk/directories/)) — these are a key source for placing a person at an address between census years.

### Military records
- Relevant conflicts during the period: Napoleonic Wars (ending 1815, just before the window); no major conflict directly affecting Scotland 1820–1860.
- UK-level collections returned by FamilySearch include: British Royal Navy Ships' Musters 1739–1861 (280,357 records); Chelsea Pensioners' Service Records 1760–1913; Merchant Navy Seamen Records 1835–1941; Militia Service Records 1806–1915.
- Campbeltown is a port town; men from the town who served at sea or in the Royal Navy would appear in naval musters and merchant records.

### Cemetery records
- Kilkerran graveyard is the historic burial ground for Campbeltown. Two published surveys exist in the FamilySearch Library catalog:
  - *An historical and genealogical tour of Kilkerran graveyard* by Angus Martin (FamilySearch Library)
  - *Kilkerran graveyard revisited* by Angus Martin (FamilySearch Library)
- Online: [Scotland, Burial Monument Inscriptions, 1507–2019](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/62497) at Ancestry ($); [Scotland, Gravestones and Memorials, 1521–2020](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/70948) at Ancestry ($); BillionGraves Scotland index at FindMyPast.
- A Campbeltown poorhouse also had a burial ground; sexton records, if they survive, would be at Argyll and Bute Archives.

### Newspaper records
- **The Campbelltown Journal:** A compiled index of births, marriages and deaths reported in this paper 1851–1855 was produced by Stuart Farrell and is held at the FamilySearch Library (not online). This is the only known indexed newspaper source for Campbeltown in this period.
- The Scotsman (Edinburgh) digital archive 1817–1950 is available at [archive.scotsman.com](http://archive.scotsman.com/) and via Ancestry; it occasionally carried Argyllshire notices.
- FindMyPast carries Scotland Newspaper Birth Notices, Marriage & Anniversary Notices, and Death Reports & Obituaries indexes (subscription).

### Immigration/emigration records
- Campbeltown was a port on the Kintyre Peninsula. Emigration from the region to Canada, Australia, and the United States was significant, particularly after the Highland and Island Emigration Society assisted departures to Australia (1852–1857, recorded on ScotlandsPeople).
- Relevant collections: Ships from Scotland to America 1628–1828 (Ancestry); Scottish Emigration Database (University of Aberdeen).
- Naturalizations filed in the United States or Canada by persons who emigrated from Campbeltown may name birthplace and parents.

### School records
- Two school record volumes for Campbeltown are digitized on FamilySearch:
  - CH3/1421/13: November 1852–October 1874 (111 images, fulltext searchable)
  - CH3/1421/12: October 1858–October 1874 (24 images, fulltext searchable)
- These are associated with the United Presbyterian congregation and record children's attendance, which can establish family presence in the town.

### Other record types
- **Argyll and Bute Archives family history sources:** The Argyll and Bute Archives (Lochgilphead) holds an extensive range of local materials — estate records, burgh records, poor registers, an index to the 1851 census of Campbeltown parish, and registers of St Kieran's Episcopal Church. The full list is documented on the [Argyll and Bute Archives Family History Sources wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Argyll_and_Bute_Archives_Family_History_Sources).
- **Statistical Accounts of Scotland:** The First (1791–1799), Second (1834–1845), and Third Statistical Accounts describe the parish, its economy, religions, and people. Available at [stataccscot.edina.ac.uk](https://stataccscot.edina.ac.uk/static/statacc/dist/home).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Relevant coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|
| ScotlandsPeople.gov.uk | OPR index 1553–1854; Statutory Registers 1855 to present (births to 1922, marriages to 1947, deaths to 1972); all censuses 1841–1921; probate 1513–1901; valuation rolls 1855+ | Subscription (~£7.50/30 credits; index free) |
| FamilySearch.org | Scotland Marriages 1561–1910 (free index, includes OPR); Scotland Births and Baptisms 1564–1950 (free index); Scotland Civil Registration 1855–1875/1881/1891 (index and images at FamilySearch Centers); 1841 and 1851 Scotland Census (free index) | Free index; images at FamilySearch Centers |
| Ancestry.com | Select Counties, Scotland, Church of Scotland, Marriages 1615–1854 (index and images); 1841, 1851, 1861 Scotland Census; Scotland Burial Monument Inscriptions; various Scotland court and criminal indexes | Subscription |
| FindMyPast.com | Scotland Parish Marriages & Banns 1561–1893; Scotland Modern and Civil Marriages 1855–2019; 1841/1851/1861 Census; Scotland Newspaper Marriage Notices | Subscription |
| MyHeritage.com | Scotland Marriages 1561–1910 | Subscription |
| ScottishIndexes.com | Scottish Paternity Index; mental health; poor relief; criminal database | Free index |
| National Library of Scotland | Scottish Post Office Directories 1773–1911; historical maps | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 45 digitized volumes match Campbeltown for 1820–1860; all 45 were returned in the single search page and are detailed above.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Records of Scotland / ScotlandsPeople Centre, Edinburgh | Original OPR registers; all Statutory Register originals; Census returns; Kirk session records | In-person (£15/day) or via ScotlandsPeople.gov.uk |
| National Archives of Scotland (NRS), Edinburgh | Nonconformist church records (CH3/1047, CH3/1421); Kirk session records (CH2/50); poor law records (HR/67); Estate and heritor records | In-person or via FamilySearch (digitized volumes) |
| Argyll and Bute Archives, Lochgilphead | Burgh records; estate papers; Episcopal church registers (St Kieran's); compiled indexes; poor registers | In-person or correspondence |
| FamilySearch Library, Salt Lake City | Microfilm copies of OPR (films 1041003–1041005); Census films; microfiche OPR index (fiche 6900069 for Campbeltown marriages); FamilySearch Center access worldwide | Free at Family History Library and FamilySearch Centers |
| Local churches | Some records may remain with current congregations | Contact current minister; appointment required |

## Records NOT online
- Original OPR register images for Campbeltown (microfilm 1041005) can only be viewed at a FamilySearch Center or Affiliate Library, or at ScotlandsPeople; they are not openly browsable online.
- St Kieran's Episcopal Church registers (baptisms 1848–1855, marriages 1849–1853) are held at Argyll and Bute Archives and are not digitized in any online collection identified in this survey.
- Campbeltown Journal birth/marriage/death notices 1851–1855 (the Farrell compilation) are held only at the FamilySearch Library in Salt Lake City.
- Post-1875 Statutory Registers (except 1881 and 1891) are available only on ScotlandsPeople or in person at the ScotlandsPeople Centre.
- Campbeltown burgh and estate records at Argyll and Bute Archives are largely physical-only.

## Known record losses
- No major courthouse fire or disaster is documented for Campbeltown parish records in the tools consulted.
- The Roman Catholic parish records before 1879 are completely lost — the wiki page for Campbeltown states: "No records are known to survive before 1879. Presumably earlier records were kept but lost." ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Campbeltown,_Argyllshire,_Scotland_Genealogy#Campbeltown_Roman_Catholic_Church))
- OPR death/burial records are very sparse: only about 20 entries before 1808 and only 32 entries 1817–1854. For that period, cemetery inscriptions and kirk session records are the best substitutes.
- OPR marriage records have a blank period for the Lowland congregation: a single entry for April 1792, then nothing until after 1792–1808 when entries resume. For this specific gap the nonconformist registers and kirk session minutes are the only alternatives.

## Research tips

- **The marriage of Hugh Mclachlan and Catharine Muir almost certainly predates 1 January 1855,** since their eldest known child was born May 1850. The OPR marriage index at ScotlandsPeople and the free index [Scotland Marriages, 1561–1910](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1771074) on FamilySearch are the first searches to run. If not found there, the nonconformist registers (Relief/United Presbyterian and Free Church) must be checked — a negative OPR result does not rule out a valid marriage.

- **The OPR index covers only Church of Scotland entries.** Nonconformist marriages were not indexed in the OPR system. The United Presbyterian (CH3/1421) and Free Church (CH3/1047) records are digitized on FamilySearch as fulltext-searchable images — the researcher should browse or use fulltext search within those volumes for the couple's names. [Scotland Church Records wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Scotland_Church_Records)

- **The 1851 census (78% indexed on FamilySearch)** will show the McLachlan family if they were resident in Campbeltown with their infant Neil; it should record ages, occupations, birthplaces, and every household member. This can confirm whether Hugh and Catharine were already married by April 1851. [Scotland Census wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Scotland_Census)

- **Kirk session minutes (CH2/50) are fulltext searchable** on FamilySearch and cover 1821–1868 for Campbeltown. A prenuptial appearance before the session, or a discipline case, may name the couple and sometimes records the marriage itself even when the OPR entry is missing. [Campbeltown Kirk Session Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Campbeltown,_Argyllshire,_Scotland_Genealogy#Established_Church—Kirk_Session_Records)

- **Scottish naming customs:** The pattern — first son for paternal grandfather, second son for maternal grandfather — suggests Neil McLachlan (1850) may carry Hugh's father's name, and James McLachlan (1852) may carry Catharine Muir's father's name. Searching for a Neil McLachlan in Argyllshire OPR births, and a James Muir, can help locate both sets of grandparents. [Scotland Naming Customs](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Scotland_Naming_Customs)

- **Mc/Mac and spelling variation:** The OPR index notes that "Mc" or "Mac" surnames may be filed at the end of the M section. On ScotlandsPeople and FamilySearch, search both McLachlan and Maclachlan, and try Lachlan, Laughlan, and other variants. Muir is fairly stable but may appear as Mure.

- **Neglected Entries Register:** Late-registered births, marriages, and deaths from approximately 1820–1860, registered 1860–1868, are on microfilm and digitized in the [FamilySearch Catalog (catalog entry 103538)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/103538). This is worth checking if the event is not found in the standard OPR or Statutory series. [Scotland Civil Registration wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Scotland_Civil_Registration)

- **ScotlandsPeople is the most comprehensive single source** for Scottish vital records. The OPR index, Statutory Registers, census, and probate index are all searchable there for a modest per-image fee. For budget-conscious research, start with FamilySearch's free name indexes to identify the likely entry, then purchase the image on ScotlandsPeople.

- **Post Office Directories** for Argyllshire and the Kintyre area (1773–1911 at the National Library of Scotland) list householders, tradespeople, and professionals by name and address — useful for placing Hugh between census years and identifying his occupation.

The locality guide (loc_001) for Campbeltown, Argyll, Scotland (1820–1860) is already in the project. Key points from it:

Please create a sequenced research plan targeting FamilySearch collections for Scottish OPR marriages, nonconformist congregation marriage records, Scottish civil registration (1855+), and the 1851 Scotland census, to find when and where Hugh Mclachlan and Catharine Muir married.

## Marriage of Hugh McLachlan and Catharine Muir: Proof Summary

**Research Question:** When and where did Hugh Mclachlan marry Catharine Muir, the parents of Neil (born 25 May 1850) and James (born 7 December 1852), both christened in Campbeltown, Argyll, Scotland?

**Conclusion:** The evidence strongly supports that Hugh McLachlan married Catharine (also recorded as Catherine) Muir on 30 May 1845 at Kilninian and Kilmore, Argyll, Scotland.

---

### OPR Marriage Index — Direct Evidence

The "Scotland, Marriages, 1561-1910" collection on FamilySearch is a derivative index of Church of Scotland Old Parochial Registers. An entry in this collection records Hugh McLachlan as groom and Catherine Muir as bride, married 30 May 1845 at Kilninian and Kilmore, Argyll, Scotland.[^1] This entry directly answers the research question. The source is a derivative index; it preserves primary information supplied by the parties themselves at the time of the marriage. The underlying original OPR marriage register page for Kilninian and Kilmore (FamilySearch image ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSHD-682W) was actively sought but returned HTTP 403. The same image is accessible at ScotlandsPeople (scotlandspeople.gov.uk) via pay-per-view subscription, a handoff not completed by the tools used in this project. Viewing the original would be expected to confirm the indexed entry.

### 1851 Scotland Census — Independent Corroboration

The "Scotland, Census, 1851" collection on FamilySearch records Hugh Mclachlin, age 32, a fisher born in Midlothian, and his wife Cathrine Mclachlin, age 27, born in Argyll, residing together in Kintyre (Cantyre), Argyllshire, Scotland.[^2] Three children appear in the household: Flora (approximately age 4), Agness (approximately age 2), and infant Niel. This is a derivative transcription of the original census enumerator's return. Residence and census facts are primary information recorded by the enumerator; biographical details (ages, birthplaces, marital status) are indeterminate in quality, supplied by an unknown household member. Flora's approximate birth year of 1847, calculated from her census age, is consistent only with the parents having married no later than approximately 1846 — corroborating the 30 May 1845 date from the marriage index. The marital status is recorded as MARRIED. The census is independent of the marriage index in record type, creating institution, and informant, and provides corroboration for the marital union at a point six years after the indexed marriage.

### OPR Christening Records — Identity Corroboration

Two derivative index entries from the "Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950" collection independently name Hugh McLachlan and Catharine/Catherine Muir as co-parents of children christened in Campbeltown, Argyll. First, the christening of Neil McLachlan (born 25 May 1850, christened 24 October 1851) names Hugh McLachlan and Catharine Muir as parents, with the presenting parent supplying primary information.[^3] Second, the christening of James McLachlan (born 7 December 1852, christened 20 June 1853) likewise names Hugh McLachlan and Catherine Muir as parents.[^4] These two records are independent of each other and of the marriage index in record type, creating institution (Campbeltown parish vs. Kilninian and Kilmore parish), and informant. Both records confirm the maiden surname Muir as reported in the marriage index, corroborating the identity of the bride.

### Nil Searches

No competing marriage entry and no contradicting evidence was encountered across any searched source.

The bride's given name appears as Catherine (sources 1 and 4), Catharine (source 3), and Cathrine (source 2, where she is enumerated under her married surname). The groom's surname appears as McLachlan (sources 1, 3, and 4) and Mclachlin (source 2). These are consistent nineteenth-century orthographic variants and do not reflect any conflict in the identity of the parties.

### Assessment

Three independent record sources corroborate the marriage index entry for Hugh McLachlan and Catherine Muir, 30 May 1845, Kilninian and Kilmore, Argyll. All four sources used are derivative indexes or transcriptions; the underlying original OPR marriage register was sought but is accessible only via a pay-per-view subscription service. No conflicting evidence was found. Viewing the original register image would be expected to confirm, not alter, the indexed entry. The evidence strongly supports the conclusion that Hugh McLachlan married Catharine Muir on 30 May 1845 at Kilninian and Kilmore, Argyll, Scotland.

**Research Answer: When and where did Hugh McLachlan marry Catharine Muir?**

**30 May 1845, Kilninian and Kilmore, Argyll, Scotland** (a parish on the Isle of Mull).

This was found in the Scotland Marriages, 1561–1910 index on FamilySearch (proof summary ps_001, tier: **Probable**), corroborated by:

| Source | Finding |
|---|---|
| OPR marriage index (src_001) | Hugh McLachlan + Catherine Muir, 30 May 1845, Kilninian and Kilmore, Argyll — direct answer |
| 1851 Scotland census (src_002) | Married couple in Campbeltown with daughters Flora (~b.1847, Argyll) and Agnes (~b.1849, Argyll) and infant Niel — confirms married before ~1846 |
| Neil's christening, 1851 (src_003) | Names Hugh McLachlan + Catharine Muir as parents in Campbeltown |
| James's christening, 1853 (src_004) | Names Hugh McLachlan + Catherine Muir as parents in Campbeltown |

**Why "Probable" and not "Proved":** Every available source is a derivative transcription or index rather than the handwritten original register page. The original Kilninian and Kilmore OPR volume exists at **ScotlandsPeople** (scotlandspeople.gov.uk) behind a pay-per-view subscription; it was actively sought but inaccessible here. Viewing that image would be expected to confirm the entry and raise the conclusion to "Proved."

**New discovery:** The 1851 census revealed two daughters not previously in the tree — **Flora McLachlan** (born ~1847, Argyll) and **Agness McLachlan** (born ~1849, Argyll) — both added as stub persons (I1, I2) for future research.

**Nil searches:** Church of Scotland Kirk Session minutes (CH2/50), Relief/United Presbyterian Church (CH3/1421), and Free Church Lochend (CH3/1047) were all searched and returned no marriage entry for this couple, consistent with the marriage having occurred in Kilninian and Kilmore (Mull) rather than Campbeltown.

guardrail_shadow_violations.detail: person_evidence link written for new tree person(s) I1, I2 with no prior same_person call: a brand-new identity should be scored before it is asserted (person-evidence/SKILL.md doctrine; issue #963). Score them with the project-relative form, which assembles both documents for you: `same_person({ projectPath, assertionId, treePersonId: "I1" })`. `assertionId` is the assertion the link cites. The tool resolves the record itself and builds the tree side as that person's matching mob, so you hand-build nothing (person-evidence, 'Call it with references, not documents'). If this call was denied, the entire batch was rejected — including any ops in other sections — and must be re-issued after the same_person call. A relationship or marriage assertion names two parties and gets a link for each. The call is about the assertion's own `record_role` party by default; for the OTHER party add `recordRole` (or `recordPersonaId`) naming it. Reusing the first party's persona for the second is how a near-zero score gets manufactured and then explained away. If the tool answers that the record holds no persona for that party, or that the candidate is a stub minted from the very persona you would be scoring (circular), say so in the link's `rationale` and proceed — the gap is still recorded; the rationale is the record of why, not a waiver. How the assertion was RETRIEVED is not such a case: a full-text hit, an image, a PDF and a sidecar-less search are all scorable, because the tool derives the record side from the record's own assertions when it cannot fetch a document. A locally-minted tree id is NOT such a case: it scores on document content and must be scored.
